title: Responses API direct vs agents
summary: Calling the Responses API from your own code gives an ephemeral agent: the definition lives in your app, nothing is created in Foundry, yet you still use Foundry models, tools, OBO auth and project governance.
useIf: The agent already runs in your own process and the definition should ship and version with the application.
avoidIf: You want Foundry to host, version, publish or give a stable endpoint to the agent.

explain.md: The runtime has three objects: an **agent** (reusable model, instructions and tools), a **conversation** (persisted input and output items) and a **response** (one execution) [[tr1]]. A response can run with or without the other two, so the lightest design is a response alone [[tr1]]. When you call the Responses API directly, the agent's instructions, tools and model live in your code. Each call assembles the agent in your process, so there is nothing to create, update or delete in Foundry [[r1]].

You still get catalog models, platform tools, project-scoped data, On-Behalf-Of authentication and project-level observability and governance through your project endpoint [[r1]]. What you give up is Foundry hosting, a versioned agent resource and the publishing flow that hangs off it. **State is a dial:** use a conversation for server-side history, reference a previous stored response, or resend earlier items [[tr1]]. Resending grows the input each turn. Ephemeral does not mean stateless: it only means the definition is not stored in Foundry. The trade-off is ownership. You must keep the definition consistent across app instances, secure the calling process and decide how to version changes, which a Foundry agent resource would otherwise do for you.

options.name: Responses API direct
options.summary: Ephemeral agent defined in your code.

app.why: The definition ships and versions with the application code [[r1]].

foundry.why: There is no Foundry agent resource to hold the definition.

none.why: Fine, and the app stays small.

custom.why: Your own process can hold any code you need.

mine.why: You already host the caller, so there is no new compute.

foundry.why: Foundry runs nothing for you in this pattern.

app.why: Code-first definitions are possible, but the agent still lives in Foundry.

foundry.why: A persisted, versioned resource with a stable endpoint.

none.why: Configuration covers it with nothing to maintain.

custom.why: No place for custom runtime code.

mine.why: You would still call a Foundry-run agent.

foundry.why: No containers or compute to manage.

app.why: Code is in your repo but deploys as a Foundry resource.

foundry.why: Versions, endpoint and identity are Foundry resources [[r2]].

mine.why: It runs on Foundry-managed sandboxes, not your hosts.

explain.takeaway: Where the definition lives and who runs the process decide most of the choice.

whereToUse: A product backend that embeds an agent and releases it with the rest of the application
Agents already running on another platform that need Foundry models, tools and OBO auth
Prototypes and tests where creating Foundry agent resources is overhead
Services that need project-level observability and governance without a hosted runtime

use: The definition should live in source control with the app and pass the app's code review
You already operate the process that makes the calls
You want Foundry capabilities without a resource to keep in sync
avoid: You want a stable Foundry endpoint, versions and publishing to Teams or Microsoft 365 for the agent itself
No one on the team wants to host or secure the calling process
You need a persisted agent definition that other teams or tools can discover, version and publish
flips: A non-engineering owner must edit the agent: use a prompt agent
You must run custom code but cannot host it: use a hosted agent
Context grows with each turn: move from resending items to a conversation or stored response reference

pitfalls.cause: Each call is a fresh response with no conversation, previous response reference or resent items
pitfalls.fix: Create a conversation, reference the previous stored response, or resend items on purpose [[tr1]].

pitfalls.symptom: Team expects to publish the agent to Teams from Foundry
pitfalls.cause: Publishing works on Foundry agent resources, and an ephemeral agent has none
pitfalls.fix: Create a prompt or hosted agent for the publish path [[r1]].

pitfalls.cause: Definitions are built in each process, and versions of the app drift
pitfalls.fix: Treat the definition as code: one module, pinned model, reviewed changes.

scenarios.title: Agent inside a product backend
scenarios.situation: A product team embeds an assistant in its service. The instructions and tools change with every release and the service already runs on its own compute.
constraints: Definition must version with the app
Service is already hosted and secured
unknowns: Does anyone outside engineering edit the agent?
scenarios.question: How do you build on Foundry?

options.name: Call the Responses API directly (ephemeral agent)
options.why: The definition ships with the app, and you still get models, tools, OBO and project governance without an agent resource to sync.
options.tradeoff: No Foundry-hosted endpoint, versions or publishing for the agent.

options.name: Prompt agent defined through the SDK
options.why: Foundry runs it and you get a versioned resource.
options.tradeoff: The definition now lives in two places unless the pipeline owns it.

options.name: Hosted agent
options.why: It adds a container, sandbox compute and a second deployment for logic the service already hosts.
options.tradeoff: Right when the agent code should be deployed and scaled separately.

flips.if: The agent must be published to Teams
Multiple services reuse the same agent
flips.then: A Foundry agent resource avoids copies.

scenarios.takeaway: Keep the definition where the code that depends on it lives.

scenarios.title: Org-wide assistant for Teams
scenarios.situation: A business team wants an assistant everyone can find in Teams with a stable endpoint and the ability to roll out new versions behind it. They have no developers.
scenarios.question: What do you choose?

options.name: Prompt agent published through Foundry
options.why: A Foundry agent resource gives versions, a stable endpoint and the publishing flow, with no code.
options.tradeoff: Limited to what configuration and tools can express.

options.name: Responses API direct from a custom service
options.why: No agent resource to publish, and nobody can host the service.
options.tradeoff: Right when developers own an app that embeds the agent.

options.name: Hosted agent
options.tradeoff: Needs developers and container compute for no gain.

flips.if: The assistant needs custom code later
flips.then: Move to a hosted agent and keep the published endpoint.

flips.if: Developers own the service and want review in Git
flips.then: Responses direct or a code-first prompt agent.

scenarios.takeaway: Publishing and versions belong to Foundry agent resources, not to ephemeral agents.

quiz.q: What do you still get when you call the Responses API directly with an ephemeral agent?
quiz.explain: The docs list models, tools, project data, OBO and project-level observability and governance. There is no persisted agent resource to version.

quiz.q: Which change most clearly moves you from a direct Responses call to a prompt agent?
options: A non-engineer must edit and publish the agent to Teams
The definition must ship with every app release
The calling service is already hosted
quiz.explain: Non-engineering editing and publishing need a Foundry agent resource. The other options favor keeping the definition in app code.

quiz.q: A second turn ignores the first. The app makes two Responses calls with no extra parameters. What is missing?
options: A conversation, a previous response reference or resent items
quiz.explain: Context is carried by a conversation, a reference to a previous stored response, or by resending earlier items. Model size or agent type does not add history.

flashcards.front: What is an ephemeral agent in Foundry?
flashcards.back: An agent whose definition lives in your code and is assembled per Responses API call. No Foundry agent resource is created, updated or deleted.

flashcards.front: Three ways to carry context between Responses calls?
flashcards.back: Use a conversation, reference a previous stored response, or resend earlier items. Resending grows the input each turn.
